description: Running code after render: fetching data, timers, and subscriptions.

screens.body:
Rendering paints the screen. But apps also fetch data, start timers, and listen for events — work that happens outside the render. React calls these side effects.

useEffect is where side effects live: a hook that runs your code after the component renders, keeping the render itself pure and predictable.

options: Work outside rendering, like fetching data or timers
check.question: What is a side effect?

screens.heading: Some work happens off-screen
screens.keyPoint: Render paints; effects do the off-screen work.

screens.body:
The function you pass to useEffect runs after React has painted the screen — not during. Your users see something immediately, then the data arrives.

This order is on purpose: renders stay fast and side effects never block the paint.
screens.heading: Effects run after the render

screens.body:
The second argument to useEffect is a dependency array: [count]. It tells React: re-run this effect only when one of these values changed.

No array at all means run after every render. An array means run after render, but only if something listed changed since last time.

options: Re-run the effect when count changes
check.question: What does [count] in useEffect mean?

screens.heading: The dependency array
screens.keyPoint: Dependencies = the 'when did it change?' list.

screens.body:
An empty array [] means 'no dependencies' — the effect runs once after the first render and never again. This is the classic fetch-on-load pattern.

It's also where timers and one-time subscriptions usually start.

options: Runs once after the first render
check.question: What does useEffect(fn, []) do?

screens.heading: Empty array = run once
screens.keyPoint: [] = once, right after the first paint.

screens.body:
If your effect starts something that keeps running — a timer, a subscription, an event listener — return a cleanup function. React runs it before the effect re-runs and when the component unmounts.

No cleanup on a timer means it keeps ticking after the component is gone: a classic memory leak.

options: Undoing the effect's setup: timers, listeners, subscriptions
check.question: What is the cleanup function for?

screens.heading: Cleanup: undo what you set up
screens.keyPoint: Set it up in the effect; tear it down in the cleanup.

screens.body:
Leave off the second argument entirely and the effect runs after every single render. Sometimes that's what you want, but usually it's overkill — or worse, an infinite loop if the effect sets state.

If you find yourself omitting the array, double-check whether [] or a dependency list is what you really meant.

check.question: An effect with no dependency array runs…

screens.heading: No array = every render
screens.keyPoint: No array = every render. Usually too much.

screens.body:
Most effects fall into a few buckets: fetching data on load, starting timers or intervals, subscribing to something (a chat socket, a resize listener), and syncing with the browser (document.title).

If your code doesn't touch the outside world, it probably belongs in the render or an event handler — not in an effect.

options: Fetching data when the screen loads
check.question: Which of these belongs in useEffect?

screens.heading: The usual jobs for effects
screens.keyPoint: Effects talk to the outside world.
